Stress: Stress triggers the sympathetic nervous system and the release of cortisol. Over time that can lead to hypertension, headaches and a weaker immune system (immunosuppression).
Stressors: Not all stress is bad: eustress is challenging but manageable, while distress is harmful. Stressors range from catastrophes to significant life changes to daily hassles.
Adverse Childhood Experiences: ACEs are stressful experiences during childhood (ages 0–17), in three types: abuse, neglect and household dysfunction. Childhood stress affects how the brain and body develop, raising health risks later in life.
General Adaptation Syndrome: The GAS describes the body under long stress in three stages: alarm (immediate fight or flight), resistance (still in high stress, using up reserves) and exhaustion (reserves depleted).
Responding to stress: Some people, mainly women, respond to stress by caring for others and building connections (tend-and-befriend). Coping comes in two kinds: problem-focused (change the stressor) and emotion-focused (change how you feel, used when the stressor seems uncontrollable).
When is it a disorder?: Something counts as a disorder when it meets the 3 Ds: deviant, dysfunctional (maladaptive) and distressing. Being unusual alone isn't enough. In the U.S., disorders are classified with the DSM-5.
Explanations by approach: Each perspective explains disorders its own way: biological (genes, brain chemistry), psychodynamic (unconscious childhood conflicts), behavioral (learned through conditioning), cognitive (irrational thoughts), sociocultural (culture), humanistic (lack of support and potential), and evolutionary.
A warning: Studying disorders can make you think you have them all: intern syndrome. Don't diagnose yourself or your friends.
Anxiety disorders: Anxiety disorders are persistent, excessive worry and fear that interfere with daily life. The rest of this deck covers the main types and their causes.
Phobias: A specific phobia is an intense, irrational fear of one object or situation, out of proportion to the real threat.
Agoraphobia: Agoraphobia is fear of places where escape might be hard. Its symptoms can be cognitive (fear of being trapped), physical (sweating, racing heart) or behavioral (staying home).
Panic & social anxiety: Panic disorder is repeated panic attacks plus worry about having more. Social anxiety disorder is intense fear of being judged in social situations.
Generalized anxiety disorder: GAD is constant worry about many everyday things, not one specific object or situation.
Depressive disorders: Depression is more than a bad mood: a sad, empty or irritable mood with physical and cognitive changes that affect functioning. Major depressive disorder lasts at least 2 weeks; persistent depressive disorder lasts at least 2 years with no manic episodes.
Bipolar disorders: Bipolar disorders swing between depressive and manic episodes. Bipolar I has full mania and can include psychosis; Bipolar II has milder hypomania and is less severe but more common.
Neurodevelopmental disorders: Neurodevelopmental disorders begin to appear in early childhood. They have high heritability, and teratogens such as alcohol during pregnancy are an environmental cause.
ADHD: ADHD is a persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity. Know the diagnosis rules on your slides: how many symptoms by age, symptoms before age 12, in two or more settings, for at least 6 months.
Autism spectrum disorder: ASD is called a spectrum because its symptoms range from mild to severe. Your slides give its statistics, including that it is more common in boys.
Dissociative disorders: Dissociative disorders are a loss of connection between thoughts, memories, feelings, surroundings and identity. The most common cause is severe trauma or major stress.
Dissociative amnesia: Dissociative amnesia is being unable to recall important personal information. A fugue state goes further: traveling or wandering without awareness of who you are.
Dissociative identity disorder: DID involves two or more distinct identities, called alters, each with its own memories and behaviors. It's what people mean by 'split personality,' not schizophrenia.
Schizophrenia: Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder that the DSM-5 places on a spectrum, because people experience it in different ways.
Symptoms: Positive symptoms are added experiences: delusions (of grandeur or persecution), hallucinations, disorganized speech (word salad) and movement. Negative symptoms are things missing, like flat affect or catatonic stupor.
Obsessive-compulsive & related: The DSM-5 moved OCD and related disorders (including hoarding, trichotillomania and excoriation) out of the anxiety disorders into their own category.
OCD: In OCD, obsessions are intrusive thoughts and compulsions are repeated actions. The cycle is obsession, distress, compulsion, relief, and the relief reinforces the compulsion, which is the behavioral explanation.
Hoarding: Hoarding disorder is persistent difficulty throwing things away, whatever their value, with clutter that compromises living spaces.
Trauma & stressor-related: PTSD, acute stress disorder and adjustment disorders all follow a traumatic or stressful event and differ mainly in how long they last. PTSD symptoms include hypervigilance, flashbacks and nightmares.
Eating disorders: Feeding and eating disorders are serious and can do lasting harm to the body. The two to know are anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa.
Anorexia nervosa: Anorexia is refusing to keep a minimally normal weight and an intense fear of gaining weight, even when underweight.
Bulimia nervosa: Bulimia is repeated binge eating plus behaviors to prevent weight gain, such as vomiting. It can be hard to spot because it often happens in private.
Personality disorders: Personality disorders are enduring, inflexible patterns that differ from a person's culture, begin in adolescence or early adulthood, and interfere with daily life. They're grouped into three clusters.
Cluster A: odd or eccentric: Cluster A is odd or eccentric: paranoid (distrust), schizoid (detached from relationships) and schizotypal (odd beliefs and behavior).
Cluster B: dramatic, emotional, erratic: Cluster B is dramatic, emotional and erratic: antisocial, histrionic (attention-seeking), narcissistic and borderline.
Cluster C: anxious or fearful: Cluster C is anxious or fearful: avoidant, dependent, and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (different from OCD).
History: Treatment has changed a lot: from asylums and lobotomies to deinstitutionalization in the late 20th century, when new medications let patients be treated outside hospitals.
Treatment today: Today's treatment is biomedical (medication and brain treatments) or psychotherapy, often combined in an eclectic approach. Only a doctor or psychiatrist can prescribe medication.
Medications: Psychotropic medications treat symptoms, not causes, by acting on neurotransmitters. Antidepressants (like SSRIs), anti-anxiety drugs (boost GABA), antipsychotics (block dopamine; can cause tardive dyskinesia) and mood stabilizers (for bipolar) each target different disorders.
Brain treatments: Three treatments act on the brain directly: the lobotomy (now historical), rTMS (magnetic pulses, no seizure) and ECT (a controlled seizure for extreme depression, with memory-loss risk).
Psychotherapy basics: Confidentiality is the cardinal rule, broken only when a client is a danger to self or others. Good therapy depends on cultural humility and a strong therapeutic alliance. Eysenck once found therapy no better than none, but later research shows it works.
Ethics: Therapists follow five ethical principles: fidelity and responsibility, beneficence and nonmaleficence, respect for rights and dignity, integrity, and justice.
Psychodynamic therapies: Psychodynamic therapy tries to bring unconscious conflicts to light through free association, dream interpretation and noticing resistance. Hypnosis was once used, but it isn't a valid way to recover memories.
Humanistic therapies: Carl Rogers' person-centered therapy is non-directive: the therapist listens actively and offers empathy, congruence and unconditional positive regard instead of advice.
Cognitive therapies: Cognitive therapy changes irrational thoughts through cognitive restructuring and Socratic questioning. Beck's theory explains depression with the negative cognitive triad: negative thoughts about yourself, the world and the future.
Behavioral therapies: Behavioral therapies change behavior through learning. Exposure therapy and systematic desensitization reduce fears, aversion therapy pairs a behavior with something unpleasant (as Antabuse does with alcohol), token economies reward good behavior, and biofeedback teaches control of body signals.
Cognitive behavioral therapies: These combine thoughts and behavior. CBT changes both; DBT adds skills for managing emotions and relationships; REBT directly challenges irrational beliefs.
Modes of therapy: Therapy can be individual (more personal and flexible, but expensive) or group (cheaper, and it shows people they aren't alone).
Anxiety Disorders|Causes: Anxiety disorders have causes from several perspectives: behavioral (learning fear, including by modeling others), cognitive (distorted, catastrophic thinking), biological (serotonin and GABA imbalances, plus hormones) and genetic (running in families).
Schizophrenia Spectrum|Causes: Schizophrenia has several causes: genetics, prenatal exposure to viruses, and imbalances in dopamine and glutamate. The dopamine hypothesis links positive symptoms to too much dopamine. The diathesis-stress model says stress can trigger an existing predisposition.
Feeding & Eating Disorders|Causes: Eating disorders have causes at every level: biological and genetic, social (like a family focus on perfection or weight-related bullying), cultural (industrialized cultures that prize thinness), cognitive (distorted attitudes about appearance and perfectionism) and stress.
Personality Disorders|Causes: Personality disorders come from a mix of causes: genetic predisposition, brain differences, environment (early abuse, neglect, trauma or poor attachment) and culture.
